(There are other hypothesis tests used for other parameters, like the variance or standard deviation, but
we will not cover those tests until chapter 11.)

According to the U.S. Public Interest Research Group’s Education Fund report, 65% of college students in
the U.S. have skipped purchasing textbooks for their classes due to cost, despite concerns about their grades.
A faculty organization believes the proportion is lower and collects sample data to test their claim. They
randomly select 545 students of whom 342 report having skipped purchasing textbooks for their classes. Do
the data support the faculty organization’s claim? Test at the 0.01 significance level.
The language of the problem makes it clear that we are asked to conduct a hypothesis test. We need
only identify it as test for a population proportion or a test for a population mean. If we read it
carefully, we can see the percentage of 65% is given, which is a proportion. Further, we are given a
count of the number of students who have skipped purchasing their textbooks, which is a qualitative
characteristic. Finally, we are asked to test an organization’s claim that the
65%. These all inform us that we are to conduct a hypothesis test for a population proportion.
